name: Cinnamomum zeylanicum bark extract

lead: This is an extract of the inner bark of the Ceylon cinnamon tree, described as one component of the Sepicontrol A5 cosmetic blend and mentioned in hair-care product discussions. The hoped-for payoff is a healthier scalp and fuller-looking hair.
Published work on the extract covers memory in rodents and in-vitro antioxidant and antimicrobial tests. No study of hair or scalp appearance was found.

paras: It is used as an ingredient in leave-on or rinse-off scalp and hair products, as part of a regular routine.
No hair-specific safety data were found in the sources reviewed.

chain: Ceylon cinnamon bark in a blend
angle.text: Ceylon cinnamon bark extract appears in the cosmetic blend Sepicontrol A5 and in hair-care product discussions, with the idea of supporting the scalp and follicles for fuller-looking hair. Hair or scalp studies were not found.

lead: Cinnamomum zeylanicum is an older botanical name for Cinnamomum verum, the evergreen tree of Sri Lanka known as true or Ceylon cinnamon. Its dried inner bark is the cinnamon spice.[1] Extracts of the bark are described as a component of Sepicontrol A5, a cosmetic ingredient blend.

Published research on the extract concerns non-cosmetic topics such as memory in rodents and in-vitro antioxidant and antimicrobial activity.[2][3] No study found tests it for hair or scalp appearance.
infobox: Bark of Cinnamomum verum (syn. C. zeylanicum)[1]
Component of a cosmetic blend (Sepicontrol A5)

paras: The inner bark is peeled in strips, dried into quills, and sold as sticks or powder. Cinnamon has a long history in traditional medicine, including as a digestive aid.[1]

A 2015 rodent study of a standardized aqueous bark extract examined learning and memory against streptozotocin-induced memory impairment.[2] A 2023 in-vitro study characterized nanosuspensions of the extract and evaluated antioxidant, antibacterial, cytotoxic and antidiabetic activity.[3] These are not hair studies.
No studies found for hair or scalp use. Registered human trials of cinnamon bark or extract address other conditions, for example type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome and obesity.[4][5]
